title: Pauquacumsuck / Pahquahkossit (Wading River)
summary: Pauquacumsuck, also recorded as Pahquahkossit and related forms, is the Wading River creek placename tied to the Occabuck boundary and clam-wading interpretation.
why_this_matters: Unearthing early pre-fishtail arrowheads, archaeologists identified Pahquahkossit as an Archaic period winter camp occupied as early as 2595 BC along the sheltered banks of present-day Wading River. Documenting such seasonal habitation sites demonstrates how Indigenous extended families successfully utilized and adapted to Long Island's specific ecological zones over thousands of years.
introduction_content: Pauquacumsuck is connected with the creek now known as Wading River in Riverhead, and earlier Pahquahkossit is one of its related historical forms.
history_content: Wading River placename, Occabuck boundary context, clam-wading interpretation, and archaeological landscape are brought together here, with dated placename and excavation details separated into the Historic Timeline.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Pequaockeon, Quaconsuck, Pauquaconsut, Pauquaconsuck, Paquaconsit, Pauquacumsok, Pauquacumsuck, Pahquahkossit, and Pahquahokossit. The name is interpreted as the brook or outlet where people wade for clams, or a clam-wading brook.

Why Place Names Matter

“When conditions change, place names can serve as indicators of environmental change.”

— Arctic Climate Impact Assessment, Changing Arctic: Indigenous Perspectives (2005), Box 3.2, 'Place names as indicators of environmental change', PDF page 66
vandalism_content: It is believed that Pahquahkossit has been completely destroyed by the new decommissioned Shoreham Nuclear Powerplant.
whereintheworld_content: Pauquacumsuck or Pahquahkossit is associated broadly with the Wading River salt-marsh and stream-mouth landscape. Its precise historic location remains uncertain.
